options: Because the engines become part of the final product the builder sells
Because the engines are used up during the production process
Because the engines are major, long-term investments like buildings
Because demand for the engines is unrelated to consumer demand for boats
questions.explanation: Production goods (raw materials and component parts) become part of the final product; engines installed in boats are component parts. Buildings and fixed equipment describe installations, and items used up in operations describe supplies - both support goods.

questions.stem: Rocky Mountain Motors builds pickup trucks in Alberta. Which purchase is a SUPPORT good rather than a production good?
options: Tires mounted on every finished truck
Steel used to form the truck bodies
Laptops and printers for the accounting department
questions.explanation: Support goods assist production but don't become part of the product; office equipment is accessory equipment. Engines and tires are component parts and steel is a raw material - all production goods that end up in the truck.

questions.stem: Which group lists the four types of support goods?
options: Raw materials, component parts, accessory equipment and services
Convenience, shopping, specialty and unsought products
Raw materials, component parts, installations and supplies
Installations, accessory equipment, supplies and services
questions.explanation: Support goods are installations, accessory equipment, supplies and services. Raw materials and component parts are production goods, and convenience/shopping/specialty/unsought are consumer product classes.

questions.stem: A Calgary craft brewery makes and sells beer. Which of its purchases is NOT a production good?
options: A new brewhouse building with fixed brewing tanks
questions.explanation: The building and fixed tanks are an installation - a support good that assists production. Barley, hops and yeast become part of the beer, so they are raw materials, which are production goods.

questions.stem: Which pairing of purchase and support-good category is correct for a Halifax accounting firm?
options: Desktop computers for every accountant - installations
A new office building the firm constructs - accessory equipment
An outside IT repair contract - supplies
Printer paper and paper clips - supplies
questions.explanation: Supplies are consumables such as stationery, paper clips and brooms. A building is an installation, computers and other office equipment are accessory equipment, and repair or maintenance contracts are services.

questions.stem: If consumer demand for Ford cars (a consumer product) increases, the company may increase its demand for paint-spraying equipment (a business good). This illustrates _____.
questions.explanation: Derived demand means demand for business products is derived from demand for the consumer products they help produce: more car buyers means Ford needs more paint-spraying equipment. None of the other options describes business demand driven by consumer purchases.

questions.stem: After Canadians began buying far more oat-based milk, Prairie Oat Mills in Saskatchewan saw orders from beverage makers for its processed oats double. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The mill sells a business product, and its demand rose because consumer demand for oat milk rose - derived demand. Primary demand is demand for a product category as a whole rather than a specific brand; it doesn't describe a supplier's business sales rising because consumers bought more of the final product.

questions.stem: Derived demand means that the demand for business products depends on the demand for the consumer products they help make.
questions.explanation: True. Business buyers purchase inputs and equipment because consumers want the final products; when consumer demand changes, demand for those business products follows.

questions.stem: Kodiak Fasteners sells specialty bolts to Canadian RV manufacturers. Economists forecast a sharp drop in consumer RV purchases next year. What should Kodiak expect and do?
options: Expect orders to rise, because manufacturers stockpile parts when consumer demand falls
Expect orders to fall, since its demand is derived from RV demand, and plan production and marketing accordingly
Expect no change, because business buyers' demand is independent of consumer demand
Reclassify its bolts as supplies so its sales are no longer tied to RV demand
questions.explanation: Demand for business products is derived from consumer demand, so fewer RV sales means fewer bolts ordered. Business demand is not independent of consumers, and relabelling the product's category doesn't change what drives its demand.

questions.stem: Which statement about derived demand is NOT correct?
options: It describes how consumer demand for a product rises after it receives positive reviews
It applies to business products such as raw materials, component parts and equipment
B2B marketers watch consumer markets because their own sales depend on them
A drop in consumer demand for cars can reduce demand for paint-spraying equipment
questions.explanation: Derived demand is business demand flowing from consumer demand - not consumer demand rising after good reviews (that's word of mouth). The other three statements accurately describe derived demand.

questions.stem: The Build a Bear Workshop in West Edmonton Mall sells custom made Teddy bears designed to be given as gifts for almost every occasion imaginable. For the Build a Bear Workshop, Teddy bears are an example of a:
questions.explanation: A product line is a group of closely related products that satisfy a class of needs - here, gift-giving. The product mix would be ALL of Build-a-Bear's lines, and the marketing mix is the 4 Ps (product, price, place, promotion), not a group of products.

questions.stem: A specific product with a unique brand, size or price, identified by its own stock keeping unit (SKU), is called a:
questions.explanation: A product item is one specific version of a product with a unique brand, size or price, and the SKU is its unique identifier. A product line is a group of closely related items, and the product mix is all of a company's lines.

questions.stem: Maplewood Kitchen offers its pasta-sauce line in 14 variations - different flavours, jar sizes and organic versions. The number of items within this one line describes the line's:
questions.explanation: Line depth is the number of product items within a line - here, 14 variations of pasta sauce. Width (breadth) counts how many different lines a company offers, which is a property of the product mix, not of a single line.

questions.stem: Glacier Outfitters has three product lines: jackets, footwear and backpacks. It adds six new colours to its existing jacket line. What has changed?
options: The product mix has become wider because more items were added
The width of the product mix has increased from three to nine
The jacket line has become deeper, while the width of the product mix is unchanged
The company has created a fourth product line
questions.explanation: Adding variations within an existing line increases that line's depth (and the total number of items), while width - the number of different lines - stays at three. Only adding a new line, such as tents, would widen the mix.

questions.stem: Lakeshore Foods wants to serve more of its frozen-pizza customers' needs without entering a new product category. Which move deepens its product line?
options: Add gluten-free, family-size and spicy versions of its frozen pizzas
Drop two pizza varieties to simplify its offering
Launch a new line of frozen desserts
License its brand name to a cookware manufacturer
questions.explanation: Deepening a line means adding items within the existing line, such as new versions of frozen pizza. Launching frozen desserts would add a new line and widen the product mix, licensing is a branding strategy, and dropping varieties makes the line shallower.

questions.stem: Line depth is the number of product items within a line, whereas the total number of items is referred to as product line _____.
questions.explanation: Per the course definitions, depth = number of items within a line and length = the total number of items. Width and breadth both mean the number of different lines in the product mix, not a count of items.

questions.stem: All of the product lines offered by a company make up its _____.
questions.explanation: The product mix is all the product lines a company offers, measured by its width (breadth). The marketing mix is the 4 Ps, and a product line is just one group of closely related products within the mix.

questions.stem: Procter & Gamble sells Pampers (baby care), Tide and Bounce (fabric and home care), and Head & Shoulders and Old Spice (beauty, health and grooming). Counting how many different lines P&G offers measures its product mix:
questions.explanation: Product mix width (breadth) is the number of different product lines a company offers. Depth is the number of items within a single line, and length is the total number of items - neither counts lines.

questions.stem: Northern Pantry Foods sells 4 cereals, 6 soups and 3 sauces, each group forming its own product line. It is about to launch a new line of 5 frozen pizzas. After the launch, what is the width of its product mix?
questions.explanation: Width = number of different product lines. Before the launch there are 3 lines (cereals, soups, sauces); adding frozen pizzas makes 3 + 1 = 4. The figure 18 (4 + 6 + 3 + 5) counts items, not lines, so it is not width.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Tim Hortons' product mix is its product, price, place and promotion.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: That describes brand equity; the product mix is the value a brand name adds
Nothing is wrong, because the product mix and the marketing mix are the same concept
That describes a product line; the product mix is the number of items within one line
That describes the marketing mix; the product mix is all the product lines a company offers
questions.explanation: The 4 Ps are the marketing mix. The product mix is the full set of product lines a company offers (for Tim Hortons, lines such as hot beverages, cold beverages, baked goods and lunch items). The number of items within one line is depth, not the mix.

questions.stem: Adding a new scent of Old Spice deodorant widens Procter & Gamble's product mix.
questions.explanation: False. A new scent is another item within an existing line, so it deepens that line. The product mix becomes wider only when the company adds a new product line.

questions.stem: A name, phrase, symbol or design, or a combination of these, uniquely given by a company to a product to distinguish it from the competition is a:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of a brand, which needs to be developed and nurtured by marketing activity. A trademark is the LEGAL protection of a brand name or mark - not the brand itself - and brand personality is the set of human traits linked to a brand.

questions.stem: Customers recognize both the spoken name 'Aurora Air' and the airline's symbol of three green northern-lights waves. The three-wave symbol is the airline's:
questions.explanation: The brand mark or logo is the part of a brand that cannot be spoken, such as a symbol or design. 'Aurora Air' is the brand name because it can be spoken.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a brand NAME rather than a brand mark?
options: A beaver symbol on a clothing label
questions.explanation: A brand name is the part of a brand that can be spoken, including words, letters and numbers - so '7-Eleven' is a name. The swoosh, the beaver symbol and the apple silhouette are designs that can't be spoken, which makes them brand marks.

questions.stem: Once a company has created a brand name and logo, the brand will hold its strength on its own without further marketing activity.
questions.explanation: False. A brand needs to be developed and nurtured by marketing activity on an ongoing basis; because brands are assets, marketers must keep investing to maintain their value.

questions.stem: Which statement about brands is NOT accurate?
options: A brand must be developed and nurtured by marketing activity
A brand can combine a name and a symbol
Only for-profit companies can have brands
A brand distinguishes a product from competitors' products
questions.explanation: Non-profits brand themselves too - MADD is one of the course examples. The other statements match the definition: a name, phrase, symbol or design (or a combination) that distinguishes a product and must be nurtured by marketing.

questions.stem: In class, students complete the sentence 'Tim Hortons is ____.' Most write 'Canadian', 'hockey' or 'Roll Up To Win'. These responses reveal Tim Hortons':
questions.explanation: Brand associations are the thoughts and feelings linked to a brand in memory, and together they form the brand image. Brand equity is the added value those associations help create - a result, not the associations themselves.

questions.stem: The thoughts, feelings and perceptions consumers link to a brand in memory are called:
questions.explanation: Brand associations - together, the brand image - are what comes to mind when consumers think of the brand. A brand advocate is a person who recommends the brand, and a brand mark is the unspoken symbol.

questions.stem: According to the course, what most fundamentally makes a brand different from a product?
options: Its substance - authenticity - and the key associations people hold about it
Its physical features, such as size, colour and materials
Its registration with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office
Its price, since branded items always cost more than products
questions.explanation: The course stresses that the difference between brand and product is substance (authenticity) and the brand's key associations. Physical features belong to the product itself (the actual layer), and registration is a trademark, which protects a brand but doesn't define it.

questions.stem: Endy, an online mattress company, finds many shoppers doubt that a mattress shipped in a box can be comfortable. Using the idea that brands provide an 'educational' opportunity, Endy should:
options: Teach shoppers why they should care - explaining how the mattress is made and why it performs - to reshape perceptions
License its name to a furniture retailer to escape the negative perceptions
Stop advertising and let the mattress's features speak for themselves
Cut its price below every competitor so that perceptions no longer matter
questions.explanation: Brands provide an 'educational' opportunity: teach people why they should care, because perceptions are important to brand relationships. Ignoring perceptions, competing on price alone, or handing the name to a licensee doesn't build the relationship.

questions.stem: Marketers need to understand a brand's key associations because consumer perceptions shape their relationships with the brand, even when those perceptions differ from the product's technical facts.
questions.explanation: True. Perceptions are important to brand relationships, so marketers study a brand's key associations (for example, how H&M, Gap and Zara are each seen) and use marketing to educate people about why they should care.

questions.stem: _____ is/are used to legally protect the written word, a sound recording, or a form of communication from being copied by another.
questions.explanation: Copyrights protect original written works, sound recordings and forms of communication (music, literature, performances) from being copied; per the course material, protection lasts the creator's lifetime plus 50 years. Trademarks protect brand names and marks, while brand loyalty and brand personality are marketing outcomes, not legal protections.

questions.stem: Bow River Brewing registers its brand name and grizzly-bear logo with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office so competitors cannot use them. The brewery is obtaining a:
questions.explanation: A trademark gives the owner the exclusive legal right to use a brand name or brand mark; in Canada it is registered with CIPO for 10 years and is renewable. Copyright protects creative works such as songs or text, and a patent protects inventions.

questions.stem: According to the course material, how long does copyright protection last in Canada?
options: 20 years from the date of filing
questions.explanation: The course material and test bank state lifetime plus 50 years, so that is the exam answer. (Canadian law moved to life plus 70 years effective December 30, 2022, but the course has not adopted that figure.) '10 years, renewable' is the trademark registration period.

questions.stem: Kestrel Labs in Calgary invents a new battery-cooling mechanism, writes a training manual about it, and names the product 'CoolCell'. Which match of asset to legal protection is correct?
options: Mechanism - trademark; manual - copyright; name - patent
Mechanism - patent; manual - trademark; name - copyright
Mechanism - patent; manual - copyright; name - trademark
Mechanism - copyright; manual - patent; name - trademark
questions.explanation: Patents protect inventions, copyright protects original written works, and trademarks protect brand names and marks. Each wrong option swaps at least one protection onto the wrong kind of asset.

questions.stem: Which of the following would NOT be protected by copyright?
options: A song written for a radio commercial
A novel by a Canadian author
A sound recording of a live comedy performance
questions.explanation: A brand name is protected by a trademark, which gives the exclusive right to use a brand name or mark. Songs, written works, sound recordings and performances are exactly what copyright protects.

questions.stem: If we consider brands to be assets, then it is critical that marketers:
options: Invest money to maintain their value.
questions.explanation: Because brands are assets, they lose value without upkeep, so marketers must invest money to maintain their value - which is why brands like those on Interbrand's ranking keep spending on quality and marketing. Selling them or constantly building new ones throws away value already built, and balancing against liabilities is an accounting idea, not a marketing action.

questions.stem: The added value a brand name gives to a product beyond its functional benefits is called:
questions.explanation: Brand equity is the added value a brand name brings beyond functional benefits, giving a competitive advantage and allowing higher prices. Brand loyalty is an individual's favourable attitude and repeat purchase - a source of equity, not the equity itself.

questions.stem: Shoppers at a Calgary outlet will pay $95 for a Roots hoodie but only $40 for an unbranded hoodie made in the same factory from the same fabric. The $55 difference reflects:
questions.explanation: Brand equity is the added value a brand name brings beyond functional benefits, which allows a higher price. Loyalty (an individual's repeat purchase and favourable attitude) can contribute to equity, but the price premium itself is the equity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes brand equity from brand loyalty?
options: Equity is the added value a brand name brings to a product; loyalty is a consumer's favourable attitude and repeat purchase over time
Equity is a consumer's repeated purchase of a brand; loyalty is the legal value of a registered trademark
Equity applies only to services; loyalty applies only to physical goods
Equity is the set of human traits linked to a brand; loyalty is the number of brands a firm owns
questions.explanation: Brand equity is the value the brand name adds (a property of the brand); brand loyalty is a favourable attitude toward and consistent purchase of a brand over time (a behaviour of consumers). Human traits describe brand personality, and legal value relates to trademarks.

questions.stem: Why does strong brand equity matter to a company?
options: It guarantees that no new competitors will enter the market
It legally prevents other firms from copying the product's design
It provides a competitive advantage and allows the company to charge higher prices
It removes the need for any further marketing investment in the brand
questions.explanation: Brand equity creates competitive advantage and price premiums. It does not remove the need for investment - brands are assets that must be maintained - and legal protection comes from trademarks and patents, not from equity.

questions.stem: A set of human characteristics associated with a brand name is called brand _____.
questions.explanation: Brand personality is the set of human characteristics linked to a brand (rugged, sincere, sophisticated). Equity is the added value of the name, loyalty is a consumer's attitude and repeat purchase, and licensing is renting the name to another firm.

questions.stem: Trailhead Gear's ads feature a weathered, adventurous character who laughs at bad weather, and the company describes its brand as 'rugged, honest and outdoorsy.' Trailhead is building its:
questions.explanation: Describing a brand in human terms - rugged, honest, outdoorsy - is building brand personality. Equity and loyalty may follow from a strong personality, but the human traits themselves are the personality.

questions.stem: Survey respondents describe Velvet & Co. cosmetics as 'sophisticated, glamorous and confident' and say they think of 'Paris' and 'luxury department stores' when they hear the name. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The responses describe the consumers' own personalities, so they say nothing about the brand
All of the responses are brand equity, because they describe the brand's financial value
'Paris' and 'luxury department stores' are brand personality traits because they are associations
'Sophisticated, glamorous and confident' are brand personality traits, which form part of the broader brand image
questions.explanation: Brand personality is the set of HUMAN characteristics linked to a brand, and it is one kind of brand association. 'Paris' and 'luxury department stores' are associations but not human traits, and equity is the added value those associations create.

questions.stem: Lumen Bank wants young Canadians to feel an emotional connection to it, the way they would to a friend. Which tactic most directly builds brand personality?
options: Add a new line of mortgage products to its product mix
Give the brand a consistent warm, witty, approachable voice across ads and social media
Lower account fees below those of the largest Canadian banks
Register the bank's name and logo as trademarks
questions.explanation: Brand personality is built by associating the brand with human traits - tone of voice, characters, spokespeople - which helps consumers make emotional connections. Fee cuts (price), trademarks (legal protection) and new lines (product mix) don't give the brand human characteristics.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of a brand personality trait?
questions.explanation: Brand personality traits are human characteristics such as sincere, rugged or sophisticated. Being available in 2,000 stores describes distribution, not a human trait.

questions.stem: A favourable attitude toward and consistent purchase of a single brand over time is:
questions.explanation: Brand loyalty combines a favourable attitude with consistent purchase over time. Brand equity is the added value of the name, and advocacy means passing positive comments to others.

questions.stem: For 15 years, Denise in Moncton has bought only one brand of toothpaste. She feels it suits her family and never considers other brands, though she rarely talks about it with anyone. Denise demonstrates:
questions.explanation: A favourable attitude plus consistent purchase over time is brand loyalty. Denise isn't a brand advocate because she doesn't pass along comments to other people.

questions.stem: Which customer is showing brand loyalty but NOT acting as a brand advocate?
options: Tara buys whichever yogurt brand happens to be on sale each week
Sana posts an enthusiastic review of a cafe she has visited only once
Omar tells everyone at work how much he loves his new Roots jacket
Ken buys only Lululemon running gear but never discusses it with friends or online
questions.explanation: Loyalty is a favourable attitude plus consistent purchase over time; advocacy is passing positive comments to others. Ken buys consistently but tells no one, Sana and Omar are advocating, and Tara shows no loyalty at all.

questions.stem: According to the course, why do marketers work to associate brands with specific personality traits?
options: To help consumers make emotional connections with their brands, which builds loyalty
To make the core benefit tangible before purchase
To register those traits as trademarks with the government
To reduce the number of product lines they must manage
questions.explanation: The course notes that marketers associate brands with personality traits and help consumers make emotional connections - the foundation of brand loyalty. Traits can't be registered as trademarks, and they have nothing to do with the number of lines.

questions.stem: Hearth Coffee Roasters notices that many customers buy from it repeatedly only when it runs discounts, switching to rivals the rest of the time. What does this suggest about their brand loyalty?
options: It is strong, because any repeat purchase demonstrates brand loyalty
It is weak, because true loyalty combines repeat purchase with a favourable attitude over time, not just deal-seeking
It is strong, because price-sensitive buyers are the most loyal customers
It is irrelevant, because coffee is always a specialty product
questions.explanation: Brand loyalty requires a favourable attitude toward the brand and consistent purchase over time. Buying only on discount and switching otherwise shows price sensitivity, not loyalty - so Hearth should work on emotional connections, not just deals.

questions.stem: A _____ is a person who speaks well of a product by passing along comments to other people.
questions.explanation: A brand advocate speaks well of a product and passes positive comments along to others through word of mouth, reviews and social posts. 'Brand associate' sounds similar but isn't the term, and 'brand preceptor' is not a marketing concept.

questions.stem: After a great trip, Jordan from Kelowna posts a five-star review of Okanagan Kayak Tours and convinces three friends to book their own tours. Jordan is acting as a:
questions.explanation: Speaking well of a product and passing positive comments to other people is what a brand advocate does. A licensee pays to use a brand name, and brand personality refers to the brand's human traits, not a customer.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a brand advocate and a brand-loyal customer?
options: An advocate passes along positive comments to others; a loyal customer consistently buys the brand but may tell no one
An advocate owns the brand's trademark; a loyal customer only buys the product
An advocate is always paid by the company; a loyal customer is never paid
An advocate always buys the brand more often than a loyal customer does
questions.explanation: Advocacy is about talking - passing positive comments to others - while loyalty is about attitude and repeat purchase. Advocates are not defined by being paid or by how often they buy.

questions.stem: Prairie Pedal, a Saskatoon bike shop, has hundreds of satisfied repeat customers but almost no online reviews or referrals. Which goal should its next campaign pursue?
options: Convert its bikes from shopping products into convenience products
Register its store name as a copyright to protect its reputation
Turn satisfied, loyal customers into brand advocates who pass positive comments to others
Widen its product mix by adding a line of coffee drinks
questions.explanation: Prairie Pedal already has loyalty; what's missing is customers speaking well of it to others - brand advocacy. Changing the product class or the mix doesn't address word of mouth, and store names are protected by trademarks, not copyright.

questions.stem: Why are brand advocates especially valuable to marketers?
options: They remove the need for the brand to be nurtured by marketing activity
They create derived demand for the brand's business products
They guarantee that the brand's equity can never decline
Their positive comments reach other consumers from a fellow customer rather than from the company
questions.explanation: Advocates spread positive word of mouth that comes from fellow consumers, which other buyers tend to find credible. They don't guarantee equity or replace the ongoing marketing a brand needs, and derived demand is a business-product concept.

questions.stem: According to the course, the purpose of experiential branding is:
options: To pair two manufacturers' brand names on one product
Not to sell you something, but to show how a brand can enrich a consumer's life
To list a product's features and price as clearly as possible
To rent the brand name to another firm in exchange for a royalty
questions.explanation: Experiential branding aims not to sell you something but to show how a brand can enrich your life, and storytelling is essential. Renting the name is licensing, pairing two names is co-branding, and listing features is a traditional sales message.

questions.stem: Lumi Outdoor opens a pop-up in Banff where visitors join free guided snowshoe walks and hear the founders' stories about growing up in the Rockies - and no one is asked to buy anything. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Showing how the brand fits into and enriches people's lives through an experience and storytelling, without a sales pitch, is experiential branding. Licensing, co-branding and mixed branding are branding strategies about who uses or owns a name.

questions.stem: Which campaign is the clearest example of experiential branding rather than a traditional sales pitch?
options: A TV ad listing the shoe's weight, cushioning and price
A free weekly run club where participants experience how the brand fits an active, social lifestyle
A cashier asking every customer to add socks to their purchase
A flyer announcing 30% off all running shoes this weekend only
questions.explanation: Experiential branding shows how the brand enriches life through experiences rather than pushing a sale. Discounts, feature-and-price ads and add-on requests are direct selling tactics.

questions.stem: Storytelling is essential to experiential branding because stories help consumers see how a brand can enrich their lives.
questions.explanation: True. The course states that storytelling is essential to experiential branding, whose goal is not to sell something but to show how the brand can enrich the consumer's life.

questions.stem: A brand manager is planning an experiential branding campaign. Which element would NOT fit this approach?
options: Activities that show how the brand enriches everyday life
An immersive event that lets visitors experience the brand first-hand
A founder's story that connects the brand to customers' values
A script focused on closing sales and maximizing units sold at each event
questions.explanation: Experiential branding is explicitly not about selling you something; a hard-close sales script contradicts its purpose. Immersive experiences, storytelling and showing how the brand enriches life are its core elements.

questions.stem: Canadian Tire's Mastercraft tools are made for Canadian Tire by outside manufacturers but sold only under the Mastercraft name in its stores. Mastercraft is an example of a:
questions.explanation: A private-label (store) brand is owned by the retailer or wholesaler, even though another company manufactures it. Who makes the product doesn't matter - ownership of the name does - and a generic product would carry no brand name at all.

questions.stem: A brand owned by the producer of the product, such as Tide or Nike, is called a _____ brand.
questions.explanation: Manufacturer (also called national) brands are owned and marketed by the producer. Private-label brands are owned by retailers or wholesalers, generic products have no brand name, and mixed branding means selling under both the firm's own and a reseller's name.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a private-label brand from a generic product?
options: There is no difference, because both terms describe store brands
A private-label product has no brand name; a generic product carries the retailer's brand
A private-label product is owned by the manufacturer; a generic product is owned by the retailer
A private-label product carries a brand name owned by a retailer or wholesaler; a generic product has no brand name
questions.explanation: Private labels such as President's Choice and Kirkland are real brands owned by resellers, while generics are unbranded, plainly packaged and low priced. Manufacturer ownership describes national brands, not private labels.

questions.stem: Maritime Biscuit Co. sells crackers under its own Maritime label and also produces crackers that a national supermarket chain sells under the chain's store brand. Maritime Biscuit is using:
questions.explanation: Mixed branding means a firm markets products under its own name and under a reseller's private-label name. Multibranding would mean using several of Maritime's OWN brand names, and co-branding would put two manufacturers' names on a single package.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of a private-label brand?
questions.explanation: Tide is owned and marketed by its producer, Procter & Gamble, so it is a manufacturer (national) brand. President's Choice, Kirkland Signature and Motomaster are owned by the retailers that sell them - private labels.

questions.stem: Samsung puts its name on its phones, televisions, refrigerators and washing machines. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Using one name for all of a company's products is multiproduct (family, umbrella or corporate) branding. Multibranding would give each product or segment a different name.

questions.stem: Procter & Gamble sells laundry detergent under three different names - Tide, Gain and Cheer - each aimed at a different segment. This strategy is:
questions.explanation: Multibranding gives each product or segment its own distinct brand name. Multiproduct branding would put one name on everything, and sub-branding would combine the P&G name with a new name.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts multiproduct branding and multibranding?
options: Multiproduct branding uses one name for all products; multibranding uses a different name for each product or segment
Multiproduct branding sells under the firm's own and a reseller's names; multibranding uses no brand names
Multiproduct branding and multibranding are two names for the same strategy
Multiproduct branding puts two manufacturers' names on one product; multibranding uses one name for all products
questions.explanation: Multiproduct (family) branding = one name across all products; multibranding = separate names for each product or segment. Two manufacturers' names on one product is co-branding, and own-plus-reseller names is mixed branding.

questions.stem: Stanley Black & Decker sells tools to homeowners under the Black & Decker name and to professional contractors under the DeWalt name. Why use multibranding here instead of one family brand?
options: Multibranding lets the company collect royalties from its own divisions
Separate names are required because tools are classified as business products
Separate names let each brand target its own segment without one brand's image diluting the other's
Multibranding lets the company avoid investing in either brand
questions.explanation: Multibranding gives each segment a brand built for it, so the professional image of DeWalt isn't blurred by the homeowner positioning of Black & Decker (and vice versa). Each brand still needs investment, nothing requires separate names, and royalties belong to licensing.

questions.stem: Multiproduct branding - also called family, umbrella or corporate branding - uses one name for all of a company's products, which makes brand extensions and sub-branding easier.
questions.explanation: True. With one name across all products (Samsung, Heinz), the company can extend that name into new product classes or combine it with new names (sub-brands).

questions.stem: Dove, long known for its beauty bar soap, launches Dove shampoo and conditioner. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: A brand extension uses a current brand name to enter a new product class - soap to hair care. Sub-branding would pair the Dove name with a new brand name, which doesn't happen here.

questions.stem: Gatorade introduces a lower-calorie drink called Gatorade G2, combining the parent brand name with a new name. This strategy is:
questions.explanation: Sub-branding combines a corporate or family brand name with a new brand name (Gatorade + G2, Porsche + Cayenne). A brand extension uses the existing name alone to enter a new product class, and co-branding requires two different manufacturers' names.

questions.stem: Northern Glow Candles is considering three launches: (1) a lavender scent added to its existing candle line, (2) Northern Glow hand soap, and (3) a premium candle range called 'Northern Glow Ember'. Which label is correct?
options: (2) is a brand extension, because the existing name enters a new product class
(1) is a brand extension, because a new item carries the existing name
(3) is a brand extension, because a new name is combined with the parent name
(2) is sub-branding, because the existing name appears on a new product
questions.explanation: A brand extension takes the current name into a NEW product class (candles to hand soap). A new scent stays in the same class and simply deepens the line, and (3) pairs the family name with a new name, which is sub-branding.

questions.stem: Using a current brand name to enter a completely new product class is called _____.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of a brand extension (Dove soap to Dove shampoo; Tide detergent to Tide stain remover). Sub-branding adds a new name to the parent name, multibranding uses separate names, and licensing lets another firm use the name for a fee.

questions.stem: Why do firms that use multiproduct (family) branding find brand extensions attractive?
options: Brand extensions let the firm sell its products under a reseller's private label
Brand extensions eliminate the risk that a weak new product could harm the brand
Consumers' existing knowledge of and trust in the brand name can carry over to the new product class
Brand extensions require a completely new brand name for each new product
questions.explanation: A brand extension borrows an established name's reputation, which makes entering a new class easier. It doesn't eliminate risk - a weak extension can hurt the family name - selling under a reseller's label is mixed branding, and a new name for each product is multibranding.

questions.stem: Tim Hortons partners with Oreo to sell a doughnut that features both brand names. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Co-branding pairs two brand names of two manufacturers on a single product. Sub-branding would combine one company's parent name with a new name, and licensing involves one firm paying to use another's name.

questions.stem: Co-branding is best defined as:
options: Marketing products under the firm's own name and a reseller's name
Pairing two brand names of two manufacturers on a single product
Allowing another firm to use a brand name in exchange for a royalty
Using one brand name for all of a company's products
questions.explanation: Co-branding = two manufacturers' brand names on one product. The other options define multiproduct (family) branding, brand licensing and mixed branding.

questions.stem: Which scenario is co-branding rather than brand licensing or sub-branding?
options: A Canadian snack maker and a national chocolate brand jointly launch a granola bar carrying both companies' names
A clothing company pays a hockey team a royalty to put the team's logo on hoodies it makes and sells
A cookware firm pays a celebrity chef's company a fee to put the chef's name on its pans
A coffee chain launches 'Summit Cold Brew', combining its own name with a new product name
questions.explanation: Two manufacturers' names jointly on one product is co-branding. Paying a royalty or fee to use another party's name (the hockey team, the celebrity chef) is licensing, and one company's name plus a new name is sub-branding.

questions.stem: Why might two manufacturers choose co-branding?
options: Each brand can borrow the other's equity and reach the other's customers
It lets a retailer own the brand name instead of the manufacturers
It lets one firm earn royalties without making any product
It removes the need for either firm to protect its trademark
questions.explanation: Co-branding lets partners combine their brand equity on one product and reach each other's customers. Earning royalties without making the product is licensing, and retailer ownership of the name is private-label branding.

questions.stem: When Nike and Apple put both of their brand names on the same running product, they are using co-branding.
questions.explanation: True. Co-branding pairs two manufacturers' brand names on a single product, as in the course's Nike + Apple and Tim Hortons + Oreo examples.

questions.stem: A contractual agreement whereby a company allows another firm to use its brand name, patent, trade secret or other property for a royalty or fee is called:
questions.explanation: That is brand licensing. Co-branding pairs two manufacturers' names on one product, mixed branding sells under the firm's own and a reseller's names, and a brand extension is the owner itself using its name in a new product class.

questions.stem: The Calgary Chinooks, a junior hockey team, allow Northern Threads to make and sell Chinooks-logo toques; Northern Threads pays the team 10% of every sale. This arrangement is:
questions.explanation: Allowing another firm to use your brand name or logo in exchange for a royalty is brand licensing. It isn't a brand extension because the team itself isn't making the toques, and it isn't co-branding because two manufacturers' names aren't being paired.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes brand licensing from brand extension?
options: Licensing always puts two manufacturers' names on one product, while an extension never does
In licensing, another firm pays to use the brand; in an extension, the brand owner itself uses its name in a new product class
Licensing applies only to patents, while an extension applies only to trademarks
In licensing, the owner uses its name in a new product class; in an extension, another firm pays a royalty
questions.explanation: Licensing is a contract letting another firm use the brand (or patent, trade secret) for a royalty or fee; a brand extension is the owner stretching its own name into a new class. Two manufacturers' names on one product is co-branding.

questions.stem: From the brand owner's perspective, what is a main benefit of brand licensing?
options: Eliminating the need to register the brand as a trademark
Removing any risk that the licensed product could affect the brand's image
Turning the brand into a generic product with no name
Earning royalty or fee income while another firm makes and sells the product
questions.explanation: Licensing generates royalty or fee income and extends the brand's reach without the owner producing the item. It doesn't replace trademark protection, and a poor licensed product can still damage the brand.

questions.stem: Alpine Cafe, famous in Canmore for its maple granola, is offered a deal: a national food company will make and sell 'Alpine Cafe Granola' in grocery stores and pay Alpine a 6% royalty. What should Alpine insist on before signing?
options: That the granola be sold as a generic product with no brand name
That the food company also print its own brand name on the package, making it co-branding
Quality controls in the licensing contract, since a poor licensed product could damage its brand
That the deal be structured as derived demand so its cafe sales rise automatically
questions.explanation: In licensing, someone else makes the product under your name, so the owner must protect brand equity through quality requirements in the contract. Adding a second name, going generic or invoking derived demand doesn't protect the brand.

questions.stem: Tide released Tide PODS; this innovation in packaging resulted in convenient, single-use pods, eliminated the need for measuring and pouring liquid detergent, and provided a hassle-free laundry experience. This demonstrates:
options: How packaging can provide a functional benefit.
How packaging can communicate the brand benefits.
How packaging can help a brand stand out.
How packaging can communicate information about the product.
questions.explanation: First and foremost, packaging has functional benefits - it allows a product to be conveniently used, and single-use pods remove measuring and pouring. Communicating information or brand benefits is a communication benefit, and standing out on the shelf is a perceptual benefit.

questions.stem: Harvest Table's redesigned cereal box adds a large nutrition-facts table, allergy warnings and step-by-step serving suggestions. These changes mainly provide which packaging benefit?
questions.explanation: Label information such as nutrition facts, warnings and directions is a communication benefit of packaging. A functional benefit would change how the product is used, stored or protected, such as a resealable liner.

questions.stem: Glacier Spring switches from a plain plastic bottle to a frosted, sculpted glass bottle so its water looks premium and catches shoppers' eyes on a crowded shelf. This change mainly delivers a:
questions.explanation: Shaping perceptions of quality and helping the brand stand out on the shelf are perceptual benefits. The bottle doesn't make the water easier to use (functional) or add label information (communication).

questions.stem: Packaging is best defined as:
options: A written statement of the manufacturer's liability for product deficiencies
The additional services that accompany a product after purchase
Any container in which a product is offered for sale and on which label information is conveyed
The part of a brand that cannot be spoken, such as a symbol
questions.explanation: Packaging is any container in which a product is offered for sale and on which label information is conveyed; labelling is an integral part of it. The other options describe a warranty, a brand mark and the augmented product.

questions.stem: A yogurt brand redesigns its tub with a resealable lid, a bold new colour scheme and clearer serving directions. Which pairing of change and benefit is correct?
options: Resealable lid - perceptual; bold colours - communication; serving directions - functional
Resealable lid - functional; bold colours - perceptual; serving directions - communication
Resealable lid - functional; bold colours - communication; serving directions - perceptual
Resealable lid - communication; bold colours - functional; serving directions - perceptual
questions.explanation: A resealable lid improves storage and usability (functional), bold colours shape perception and help the brand stand out (perceptual), and directions are label information (communication). The option pairing bold colours with communication is tempting because it gets the lid right, but colours shape perception rather than convey information.

questions.stem: A Canadian juice brand wants its packaging to signal higher quality so it can justify a premium price on a crowded shelf. Which packaging benefit should it focus on?
questions.explanation: Perceptual benefits shape how consumers perceive quality and help a brand stand out. Functional changes improve usability, communication adds information, and packaging belongs to the actual product, not the augmented layer.

questions.stem: Ease and Relax Centre, a specialty unit providing high-end massaging services, has customer testimonials on its website. By doing this, Ease and Relax Centre is dealing with the service characteristic of:
questions.explanation: A massage can't be seen or touched before purchase, so testimonials give prospective clients tangible evidence of the experience - a response to intangibility. Inconsistency is about variable quality between deliveries, and 'incongruity' is not one of the four I's.

questions.stem: The service characteristic meaning that services cannot be touched, seen or tried before they are purchased is _____.
questions.explanation: Intangibility means a service can't be touched or seen before purchase, so marketers add tangible cues. Inseparability is simultaneous production and consumption, inconsistency is variable quality, and inventory is the inability to store services.

questions.stem: Clearview Financial Planning in Calgary finds that prospects hesitate because they can't evaluate its advice before signing up. Which tactic best addresses this characteristic of services?
options: Hire part-time planners for the busy RRSP season
Offer lower fees during slow months to fill unused appointment slots
Show tangible cues such as client testimonials, credentials and a professional office
Write a standard script so every planner delivers advice the same way
questions.explanation: Not being able to evaluate a service before purchase is intangibility, which tangible cues address. Off-peak pricing and part-time staff address inventory, and standard scripts address inconsistency.

questions.stem: Rocky Lodge Hotels takes four actions. Which one targets intangibility rather than another of the four I's?
options: Posting 360-degree virtual tours and guest reviews of its rooms online
Discounting rooms on weeknights when occupancy is low
Taking online reservations to manage peak-season demand
Training all front-desk staff to follow the same check-in standards
questions.explanation: Virtual tours and reviews let guests 'see' an intangible stay before buying. Weeknight discounts and reservations manage inventory (perishable capacity), and standardized training addresses inconsistency.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four I's of services?
questions.explanation: The four I's are intangibility, inconsistency, inseparability and inventory. 'Incongruity' appears as a distractor in test-bank questions but is not one of them.

questions.stem: Customers of Summit Hair Studio rave about the senior stylist but complain that cuts from the newer stylists vary a lot from visit to visit. This problem reflects which characteristic of services?
questions.explanation: Inconsistency means service quality varies because it depends on the people who deliver it. Inseparability is tempting because a stylist is involved, but the problem described is VARIATION in quality, not simultaneous production and consumption.

questions.stem: Peak Fitness, an Edmonton gym chain, wants every personal-training session to meet the same standard no matter which trainer leads it. Which response targets the inconsistency of services?
options: Post member testimonials and before-and-after photos online
Build a more attractive, modern gym facility
Offer discounted memberships for off-peak hours
Standardize session plans and train all trainers on them
questions.explanation: Standardization and training reduce the variation that comes from different people delivering the service. Testimonials and attractive facilities are tangible cues (intangibility), and off-peak discounts manage inventory.

questions.stem: Inconsistency means the quality of a service can vary because it depends on the people who provide it.
questions.explanation: True. Because services are delivered by people, quality can differ from one employee or occasion to the next, which is why firms rely on standardization and training.

questions.stem: Which situation illustrates inconsistency rather than inseparability?
options: The same restaurant meal is excellent on Monday and poorly prepared on Friday, depending on the cook on shift
A patient must be present in the dentist's chair while the cleaning is performed
A concert is produced by the band at the same moment the audience consumes it
A client's view of a law firm is shaped by the lawyer who personally handles her case
questions.explanation: Quality that varies with who is working is inconsistency. Being present during delivery, simultaneous production and consumption, and judging the service by its deliverer all describe inseparability.

questions.stem: Why are training and standardization the main tools for managing inconsistency?
options: Services cannot be stored, so training builds up inventory for peak periods
Services are produced by machines, so standardization keeps them calibrated
Service quality depends on the people delivering it, so making their performance uniform reduces variation
Services cannot be seen before purchase, so training makes them tangible
questions.explanation: Inconsistency comes from the human element - different people deliver at different quality levels - so standard procedures and training narrow that variation. Storage problems are inventory, and invisibility before purchase is intangibility.

questions.stem: At Cedar Spa, each massage is produced by the therapist at the same moment the client experiences it, and clients judge the spa largely by the therapist who treats them. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Inseparability means consumers can't separate the deliverer of the service from the service itself, and production and consumption happen at the same time. Inconsistency would require the stem to describe quality varying between therapists or visits.

questions.stem: The service characteristic in which consumers cannot separate the deliverer of the service from the service itself is:
questions.explanation: That is inseparability - the service is produced and consumed simultaneously, so the provider is part of the experience. Idle production capacity is part of the inventory characteristic (supply exceeding demand).

questions.stem: A Calgary tutoring company notices two issues: (A) students judge the company almost entirely by the individual tutor sitting with them, and (B) lesson quality differs noticeably from tutor to tutor. Which matching is correct?
questions.explanation: Judging the service by the person delivering it is inseparability; quality differing from one tutor to another is inconsistency. The reversed option is the classic trap - ask whether the issue is 'who delivers it' or 'how much it varies'.

questions.stem: Because of inseparability, a dental clinic's patients see the hygienist as the service itself. What should the clinic prioritize?
options: Removing its brand name so patients focus only on the hygienists
Offering discounts on slow weekday afternoons to fill empty appointment slots
Hiring and preparing hygienists who create a positive experience in every patient interaction
Posting more photos of the clinic online so patients can see it before booking
questions.explanation: When the deliverer can't be separated from the service, the person-to-person encounter IS the service, so the people delivering it matter most. Photos address intangibility, off-peak discounts address inventory, and dropping the brand name helps nothing.

questions.stem: Inseparability means a service is produced first and stored, then consumed later when the customer needs it.
questions.explanation: False. Inseparability means the service is produced and consumed at the same time, and the consumer can't separate the deliverer from the service. The fact that services can't be stored relates to the inventory characteristic.

questions.stem: On weekday afternoons, Lakeview Bowling in Regina has most of its lanes empty while staff are on shift and the lights and heat are on. This costly situation is an example of:
questions.explanation: Idle production capacity occurs when the supply of a service exceeds demand, and it's expensive because costs continue while capacity goes unused - part of the inventory characteristic. Inconsistency is about varying quality, not unused capacity.

questions.stem: A Banff ski-rental shop has long line-ups on holiday weekends but sits mostly idle midweek. Which set of tactics addresses the inventory characteristic of services?
options: Write a standard fitting checklist for every rental technician
Post customer testimonials and photos of happy skiers on its website
Offer midweek discounts, take online reservations and add part-time staff on weekends
Change its name and logo to appear more premium
questions.explanation: Services can't be stored, so firms smooth demand and capacity with off-peak pricing, reservations and part-time staff. Testimonials address intangibility, and checklists address inconsistency.

questions.stem: Idle production capacity occurs when the supply of a service exceeds demand, and it is expensive for the service provider.
questions.explanation: True. When supply exceeds demand, the provider still pays for staff, space and equipment while capacity goes unused - and that unused capacity can't be stored for later.

questions.stem: Which statement about the inventory characteristic of services is NOT correct?
options: Unused capacity, such as an empty airline seat, is costly to the provider
Idle production capacity occurs when demand for a service exceeds the supply available
Fluctuating demand makes it hard to judge the capacity needed at peak times
Services cannot necessarily be stored and accessed when they are in demand
questions.explanation: Idle production capacity is the reverse: the SUPPLY of a service exceeds demand. The other statements correctly describe inventory - services can't be stored, fluctuating demand complicates peak planning, and unused capacity is expensive.

questions.stem: Why is an empty seat on a Prairie Air flight that has already departed considered a service-inventory problem?
options: The seat's capacity perished when the plane left; it cannot be stored and sold later
Passengers cannot separate the pilot from the flight they are taking
The flight attendants' service quality varied on that particular flight
Passengers could not see or touch the flight before buying a ticket
questions.explanation: Services can't be stored, so capacity that goes unused at departure is lost forever - an inventory problem. Varying quality is inconsistency, not seeing the flight beforehand is intangibility, and the pilot being part of the service is inseparability.
